narrative: The Forest Glen Subdivision Site is a 39-acre site and is located in a suburban area in Niagara County NY. The site is approximately 0.5 miles north of Porter Road with the Expressway Village mobile home subdivision adjacent to the Site's southern boundary. The site is also bound by the Railroad yard.  Access to the Site is through Edgewood Drive.The site includes one 38,400 sq. ft., one-story commercial/light-industrial building and a small shed that houses the extraction well control panel. The surrounding areas include an asphalt parking lot, maintained grass lawn, and undeveloped woodlands. The Site is bounded by highway I-90 to the north and east, Conrail Foote Railroad Yard to the west, and the Expressway Village mobile home subdivision to the south. The 39-acre Site is divided by East Gill Creek, a narrow, low-flowing creek. South of Gill Creek is the now vacant 15-acre Forest Glen Subdivision, which consisted of 51 mobile homes and two permanent residences. The southern portion of the Site includes the Edgewood Drive Wooded Lots, which are two 3-acre undeveloped wooded lots located to the north and south of Edgewood Drive. The northern portion of the Site consists of the 18-acre parcel referred to as the Northern Aspect, which includes a 15-acre undeveloped triangle of land which is bordered on the west by a berm, approximately 11 feet in height. The 1.5-acre Wooded Wetland is on the eastern side of the Northern Aspect.Current Zoning and Land Uses: The Site is currently active and is zoned for commercial/light industrial use. The surrounding parcels are currently used for a combination of residential and commercial. The nearest residential area is 340 feet to the south of the site.Past Use of the Site: During the 1970's, the low areas of the site, including a former creek bed, were filled with unknown materials. Soil sampling, performed by the Niagara County Health Department, indicated the presence of phenolic compounds, phenol formaldehyde type resin and polyvinylchloride resins in some samples.  Between 1987 and 1989, EPA investigated this site and found it to be contaminated with various organic chemicals in high concentrations. Lead and mercury were also found at elevated levels. The site was placed on the National Priorities List (NPL).Operable Units: The site was divided into three operable units. An operable unit represents a portion of a remedial program for a site that for technical or administrative reasons can be addressed separately to investigate, eliminate or mitigate a release, threat of release or exposure pathway resulting from the site contamination.Operable unit 1 (OU1) included the permanent relocation of the subdivision residences. OU2 consists of the on-site soils and sediments. OU3 addresses the groundwater plume.Contaminants of Concern (Including Materials Disposed)Contaminant Name/TypeTrichloroethene (TCE)Benzo(a)pyrenePrior to remediation, the primary contaminants of concern were volatile organic compounds (VOCs), semi-volatile organic compounds (SVOCs)(including polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAH)), and inorganics (i.e. heavy metals) in soil, PAHs, pesticides, polychlorinated biphenyls (PCBs), and inorganics (i.e. heavy metals) in wetland sediments, and VOCs and inorganics (i.e. heavy metals) in groundwater. Remedial actions have successfully achieved soil cleanup objectives for commercial use. Residual contamination in the soil, groundwater, and sediment is being managed under a Site Operations and Maintenance Plan.

narrative: The Love Canal site is an approximately 70-acre site located in a residential area at 805 97th Street in the City of Niagara Falls, Niagara County. The site is bounded by Colvin Boulevard to the north, 100th Street to the east, Frontier Avenue to the south and 95th Street to the west.The site was originally an abandoned excavation project by William T. Love, who, in the early 1890s, planned it as a power canal between the upper and lower sections of the Niagara River. The site filled with water and was used by local residents for swimming, ice skating, and other recreation purposes. From approximately 1942 to 1953, while residents were using the site for recreation, Hooker Electrochemical Company disposed of industrial hazardous waste at the site. Based on Hookerestimate upon estimates, the chemical giant dumped at least 21,800 tons of chemical wastes at this site. Those wastes included: naphthalenes, benzoyl chlorides, benzotrichlorides, Metal chlorides, liquid disulfides, Hexachlorocyclohexane (Y-BHC/Lindane), Chlorobenzenes, Benzylchlorides--including benzyl chloride, benzyl thiocyanate, dodecyl (Lauryl, Loral) mercaptans (DDM), chlorides and miscellaneous organic sulfur compounds, chlorotoluene, thionyl chloride, and trichlorophenol (TCP) containing significant amounts of 2,3,7,8-tetrachlorodibenzo-p-dioxin (TCDD, or dioxin).In 1953, Hooker sold the Canal site to the Niagara Falls Board of Education. This was soon followed by the construction of housing on 97th and 99th streets and the construction of the 99th Street School in 1954. The 99th Street School was built on and adjacent to the middle portion of the now-covered and grassed Canal. Two streets, Read and Wheatfield Avenues, were constructed to provide access to 97th and 99th Streets. Residents living adjacent to the site on 97th and 99th streets complained of minor explosions and fumes from the 1960's into the mid-1970's. Following the Blizzard of 1977, precipitation and melting snow infiltrated the Canal and apparently forced the chemical wastes to the surface in what is referred to as a bathtub effect. Contaminated surface and groundwater migrated laterally through soils and infrastructure into residential yards, basements, and the storm and sanitary sewers (some of which outfall into nearby the adjacent Cayuga Creek). Residents continued to complain of chemical odors and numerous illnesses and miscarriages. NYSDEC, NYSDOH, and USEPA eventually collected basement sump, soil, and air samples and found that significant contamination was present.In 1978, the Commissioner of the Department of Health declared the area a public threat to human health. Pregnant women and children under the age of two residing in homes adjacent to the canal were relocated to hotels and motels. The evacuation order was eventually expanded. A permanent leachate collection system, 22 acre clay cap and an activated carbon treatment plant was constructed. This remedial work was done to reduce the amount of water infiltrating into the cap, intercept laterally migrating contaminated groundwater (leachate), and treat the collected leachate for containment objectives. Effluent from the treatment processes are discharged to the Niagara Falls sanitary sewer system for additional treatment at the Niagara Falls Waste Water Treatment Plant. There is no bottom or side enclosures at the site.In 1984, a 40 mil. (a measurement of plastic sheeting, approximate 1.19 millimeters, or a thick credit card or paper clip) High Density Polyethylene synthetic liner cap (HDPE) was installed.The surrounding waterways were and are contaminated as a result of the migration from Love Canal. Chemicals migrated into Black, Bergholtz and Cayuga Creeks, the Little Niagara River, the Niagara River, as well as the 102nd Street delta into the Niagara River. Eventually, 99th Street School, another proximate elementary school, and houses on several streets were razed, creeks were partially remediated, and portions of downgradient sewers across the LaSalle section of Niagara Falls were cleaned.Occidental installed perimeter groundwater monitoring wells. There are ongoing operation, maintenance, and groundwater well monitoring activities. There is, however, no routine air, biota, surface water, or soil monitoring at Love Canal. The HDPE liner cap is now forty two years old (as of 2026).In September 1988, NYSDOH issued a Love Canal Habitability Decision Report on the Emergency Declaration Area (EDA ) of the landfill. The Habitability Study divided the area into seven parts. The Emergency Declaration Areas 4 through 7 were declared habitable for residential use. Areas 1,2 and 3 were determined to be suitable only for commercial and/or light industrial use.In 2012, hundreds of area residents brought a lawsuit contending that Love Canal chemicals were once again migrating to their homes, yards, and sump pumps. A state court judge dismissed the lawsuits in 2024 primarily on preemption grounds. A jury was never able to hear expert testimony or testing results.According to reports published in 2023, Love Canal chemical waste continues to migrate from the site to the Niagara River.

Approximately 70,000 tons of this waste was generated and disposed of on site. SKW Metals and Alloys, Inc (SKW) purchased a portion of the property and began operating a solid waste disposal facility to address ferrochromium silicon baghouse dust and ferrosilicon baghouse dust wastes. narrative: The Stauffer Chemical Plant PASNY site is a 22.91-acre site located at 5715 Lewiston Road in the Town of Lewiston, Niagara County. It is adjacent to the north side of the New York Power Authoritys (NYPA) Robert Moses Power Plant forebay canal, east of the Robert Moses Parkway and the Niagara River, south of the Riverdale Cemetery, and west of Interstate 190.      It contains the old plant site (Area A) that is about 20 acres in size and two former disposal areas (Areas B and C) that are about 2 acres in size combined.      The site is the location of the former Stauffer Chemical Company. The plant produced metallic aluminum from about 1900 to 1930. From 1930 to 1976, the plant produced carbon tetrachloride, parachlorothiophenol, metal chlorides, and a variety of industrial chemicals, including chlorine, sodium hydroxide, silicon, sulfur chloride. In 1957, Stauffer Chemical began producing trichloride, a raw material for manufacturing rocket fuel.  Methylene chloride and tetrachloroethylene were repackaged from bulk during this time period as well. Stauffer disposed of unknown quantities of asbestos, graphite, cinders, concrete cell parts, reactor linings, scrap sulfur and metal, silicon, zirconium, and titanium oxides.      Chemical operations at the facility ceased in 1976 and all structures associated with the plant were demolished in the early 1980s. Investigations revealed contamination.      In 1989, EPA and DEC issued a report prioritizing 33 site clusters in order of theirpotential for polluting the Niagara River. The 33 site clusters were divided into three categories. This site was designated as a Category II priority site with estimates of between 1 to 50 lb/day loads to the Niagara River.      Sites from Category I and II collectively represented 99.9% of the total estimated loadings of 694 lbs (315 kg)/day.      Prior to remediation, the primary contaminants of concern were carbon disulfide, carbon tetrachloride, chloroform, methylene chloride, tetrachloroethene, benzene, chlorobenzene, toluene, and trichloroethene in soil and groundwater. Remedial activities have successfully achieved soil (not groundwater) cleanup objectives for commercial use.  Residual contamination in soil and groundwater is being managed under a Site Management Plan. The only remedial system currently operating at the site is the groundwater extraction and treatment system.      Groundwater is continuously extracted and processed through a physical chemical treatment system. Periodic groundwater quality sampling is done at select monitoring wells.  Water level measurements are monitored for hydraulic contouring and containment checks.      The former plant site is fenced and capped. According to authorities, the groundwater contaminant seeps often visible on the forebay walls do not pose a contact hazard since they are not readily accessible.

narrative: The Tract II Highland Avenue Site is an approximately 13.046-acre site made up of three separate parcels in an urban area of the City of Niagara Falls, Niagara County. The western parcel is bordered by Highland Avenue and residential properties to the west, the Tract I Highland Avenue Site (BCP Site No. C932157), the Tulip Corporation Site (932170) to the north, and the delisted portion of the Tract II Highland Avenue Site to the east, and Beech Avenue and residential properties to the south. The eastern parcel is bordered by vacant industrial property to the north, a church and residential properties on 17th Street.      A fifteen-foot-wide parcel north of the delisted portion of the Tract II Highland Avenue Site connects the Eastern and Western parcels of the site.      The site is currently vacant.      Between 1903 and 1971, a series of business form companies operated on the Western parcel of the Tract II Highland Avenue Site.  Those buildings were destroyed by fire and then demolished during the 1970s. Demolition debris and re-worked native silty clay soil was used as fill material.      The Eastern parcel of the Tract II Highland Avenue Site was part of the former battery manufacturing facilities that encompassed the adjacent Tract I Highland Avenue and Tulip Corporation sites.  This area was historically used to dispose of waste and fill materials, which included building demolition debris, plastic battery casings and other granular fill materials associated with the former battery manufacturing facilities.      In 2000, Niagara Falls conducted a site investigation. The primary contaminants identified during the investigation were metals and PAHs in fill materials. Niagara Falls elected not to proceed with the remediation of the site.      In 2008, the site was listed as a Class 2 site (Site No. 932136) in the Registry of Inactive Hazardous Waste Disposal Sites in New York State (Registry). Class 2 means that the site was a significant threat to the public health or the environment, and action is required).      In November 2009, the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) fenced the site buildings to help reduce trespassing.  The EPA also removed and cleaned PCB sludge and water from a sump within the underground parking garage as part of an Emergency Removal action that was conducted in 2009 on the adjacent Power City Warehouse property.  The garage is located on the western parcel of the site and was part of the Moore Business Forms Building.      In March 2012, the Department issued a ROD Amendment that modified the remedial method from off-site disposal to on-site stabilization and placement.  Remediation of the site by the potentially responsible party began in the Fall of 2012 and was completed in 2016. In November 2018, a Certificate of Completion was issued for the site.      Prior to remediation, the primary contaminants of concern were lead, PAHs, and Technologically Enhanced Naturally Occurring Radioactive Material (TENORM) in fill material. TENORM exceeding twice background activity levels were transported off-site and disposed of at licensed disposal facilities. Groundwater was not contaminated above groundwater standards.      Residual contamination in fill material is being managed under a Site Management Plan.      A cover system was placed over the entire Western parcel and consists of a minimum 1-foot thick soil or gravel cover over a demarcation layer.      A proposed 5-acre park area, located between the Eastern and Western parcels, was remediated to restricted residential SCOs and does not contain a cover system.  This portion of the site was delisted from the Registry.      The National Grid Right of Way (ROW) that bisects the site in a north-south direction was also remediated to restricted residential SCOs and does not contain a cover system.      Residual contamination in fill material is being managed under a Site Management Plan

narrative: The Charles Gibson Site is an approximately 2.00-acre site in a commercial and residential area of Niagara Falls. Cayuga Creek borders the site to the north and east.      In the fall of 1957, Olin Chemical dumped approximately 438 drums of hexachlorobenzene and then 101 truckloads of hexachlorocyclohexane (BHC) alpha-beta cake at the site. HCB was used as a fungicide and generated as a by-product or impurity in related chemical syntheses. The alpha-beta cake was residue from Olin's manufacturing process that produced a mixture of isomeric forms, which included the alpha, beta, delta and gamma isomers of BHC. It is suspected that additional quantity and/or types of waste maybe present from Olin's manufacture of gamma-hexachlorocyclohexane(lindane) and 2,4,5-Trichlorphenoxy acetic acid.      After discovery of the site in 1980, subsequent testing revealed that soil and groundwater was contaminated. Sampling by the NYSDEC in 1982 indicated that the waste material contains BHC's in concentrations exceeding 90,000,000 ?g/kg. Olin Chemical eventually entered into a stipulated agreement with the State of New York. Olin remediated its own site between 1989 and October 1990. The remedy consisted of re-routing Cayuga Creek around and away from the waste and installation of a soil-bentonite slurry wall, a double flexible membrane liner cap, a groundwater perimeter collection drain system, and wet well/pump chamber.      Part of the site consists of a grassy capped mound surrounded by a groundwater flow cut-off wall and a perimeter collection trench to intercept groundwater migrating across the site. The collected groundwater is conveyed to a wet well/pump station and automatically pumped into the sewer system for treatment at the Niagara Falls Wastewater Treatment Plant. The capped area of the site is enclosed within chain link and stockade fencing.      Prior to remediation the primary contaminant of concern was hexachlorobenzene in soil and groundwater. Remedial actions have achieved cleanup objectives for a closed landfill. Residual contamination in soil and groundwater is being managed under a Site Management Plan.      Migration to Cayuga Creek is being minimized by a slurry wall barrier, a cap and drain system, and rerouting of the creek.      The site is currently under "Post-Closure Operation, Maintenance, and Monitoring."

This 88-acre site was once part of a larger Vanadium site that included the SKW Site (932001C) and the Airco Properties Site (932001B). It is bounded on the north by an automobile depot and vacant property, on the west by Witmer Road (Route 31), on the east by Interstate 190, and on the south by vacant land and industrial facilities. The New York Power Authority purchased the property from the Vanadium Corporation of America in 1959 for the construction of the Niagara Power Project and its associated massive underground conduits. A portion of this property was subsequently sold to the Niagara Mohawk Power Corporation.The large ground surface is elevated as a result of landfill disposal. Numerous high voltage electrical transmission towers are located on the site and overhead electrical transmission lines cross the site. The conduits run underground. The Vanadium site is also near the Union Carbide site (932035) and the Carborundum Globar site (932036), both of which are inactive hazardous waste disposal sites.The Lower Niagara River is approximately 1.4 miles to the west, the New York Power Authority (NYPA) reservoir approximately 0.8 miles to the north, and Gill Creek approximately 1,000 feet to the east.There are no active industrial operations on the property.Vanadium conducted its operations on this and its larger property from 1920 to 1964. Portions of the site were used to dispose of an estimated 594,000 tons of wood, brick, ash, lime slag (calcium hydroxide), ferrochromium silicon slag, and ferrochromium silicon dust. Waste piles reportedly contained calcium hydroxide, ferromanganese slag, ferrochromium slag, and ferrochromium dust. Rusted and crushed 55-gallon containers and scrap metal were also observed on and around waste piles on both the Airco and NiMo/NYPA properties. Contaminated fill is widespread. The thickness of the fill material generally ranges from 1 to 21 feet. The predominant fill material consists of whitish gray slag; cinders; and whitish gray, fine-grained, lime-like material. In most areas, the slag is covered by soil fill. In other areas, and before remediation, the slag was present at the ground surface.The presence of hazardous waste is confirmed. The pH values in groundwater wells and surface water exceed 12.5. Groundwater Standards were exceeded for vinyl chloride, trichloroethene, phenol, chromium, manganese, hexavalent chromium, cyanide, magnesium, sodium and zinc.Remedial action to implement the remedy started in summer 2013 and was completed in 2014. Long term monitoring is required for OU#3. There is a Site Management Plan for management of residual contamination at this site.Parts of the Vanadium site have separate listings for ongoing contamination, including e.g.,NYSDEC C932143, Northern Ethanol Redevelopment Site, 137 47th Street.

This 3.5 acre site is located within the Art Park facility (beneath the facilitys outdoor amphitheater complex), along the top of the Niagara Gorge. The site is approximately 185 feet from the edge of the Niagara River and 1000 feet south from the end of 4th Street in the Village of Lewiston.This site was once used as a quarry from 1953 to 1969. During its ownership by the Stauffer Chemical Company, the company used one of the quarry sites to dispose of wastes generated by its Lewiston Facility, including an unknown quantity of asbestos, graphite, cinders, reactor linings, scrap sulphur, metal, and silicon, zirconium and titanium oxides.  The wastes were buried in the abandoned quarry, covered, and then the park facilities were built over it. In 1957 the NYS Power Authority acquired this site and surrounding properties for the disposal of construction debris generated during the construction of a Niagara hydroelectric power generating plant approximately a half mile upstream from the site.Sampling at the site has identified the presence of heavy metals and organic contaminants in the soil and surface water at levels slightly above groundwater drinking standards. Sampling by the USGS revealed the presence of organic compounds greater than the detection level of 20 ppb for soil and 1 ppb for water. A State Superfund Phase I Investigation was completed in 1984.  The site has also been investigated by the Niagara County Health Dept. and the USEPA. They found low levels of various heavy metals and organic contaminants in soil and surface water.  This site has been filled and graded then covered (capped) by buildings, paved and stoned parking lots. In May 2011 low levels of metals were detected. Based on the above the site was reclassified and removed from the Registry on 11/28/2011.Repeated attempts to identify disposal areas and contaminants have been unsuccessful given the size of the property, although trace levels of soil and groundwater contamination have been detected. narrative: The Olin Corporation Plant Site is located at 2400 Buffalo Avenue, in an industrialized and residential area in the City of Niagara Falls, New York. The Plant is bounded by Buffalo Avenue to the north, the DuPont Chemical Corporation Plant Site to the south, the former Solvent Chemical facility to the east, and vacant land to the west. Populated residential neighborhoods are across the street to the north.The Olin Corporation Plant Site is divided into three distinct parcels.The western parcel, formerly known as Plant 1, is a 6.5 acre parcel bounded on the north by Buffalo Avenue, on the south and west by a railroad right-of-way, and on the east by lands owned by DuPont. This parcel lies across Buffalo Avenue from 24th Street. The parcel is mostly open paved areas with an Olin warehouse building located on the parcel.The middle parcel, formerly known as Plant 2, is approximately 15.6 acres and is located between Chemical Road and DuPont-owned lands to the west, and Gill Creek to the east. This parcel contains all of the current manufacturing operations. The parcel contains manufacturing and support buildings. Open areas in between are paved.The eastern parcel is approximately 5.4 acres and lies immediately east of Gill Creek. This parcel is owned by Olin, but for a time was leased to the adjacent DuPont facility.The upper Niagara River is approximately 1000 feet south of the site. Gill Creek, a tributary to the Niagara River, bisects the eastern portion of the site from north to south. Residential areas are located approximately 1000 feet north of the site.The site is currently owned and operated by Olin for chemical manufacturing (chlorine products).The plant site has been a major producer of chlorine bleaches and caustic soda by Olin and its predecessors since 1897. Chlorine and caustic soda were historically produced using mercury amalgam chlor-alkali cells, however mercury is no longer used to manufacture chlorine. Olin also produced chlorinated organic chemicals (principally chlorobenzenes and chlorophenols) in Plant 2 from 1950 to 1956.The site had significant soil and groundwater contamination.In 1989, EPA and DEC issued a report prioritizing 33 site clusters in order of theirpotential for polluting the Niagara River. The 33 site clusters were divided into three categories. This site was designated as a Category II priority site with estimates of between 1 to 50 lb/day loads to the Niagara River.Sites from Category I and II collectively represented 99.9% of the total estimated loadings of 694 lbs (315 kg)/day.Contaminants of Concern (Including Materials Disposed) include, mercury, coal fines, mercury cell brine sludges, and organic chemicals (TCP and BHC). narrative: The Witmer Road site is a 1-acre parcel in the Town of Niagara, Niagara County.  This site is located in an urban area. The site is now a scrapyard and is bordered by scrap yards. The potential for contaminant migration is indeterminable.      From the early 1950s to 1965, the Witmer Road disposal site reportedly was used to dump various types of waste including lime clean-outs from the International Mineral and Chemical Company, wastes from air pollution control equipment owned and operated by Airco Alloys, and slag materials from the Vanadium Corporation. The City of Niagara Falls reportedly operated two refuse burning pits where paper, furniture, and wood debris reportedly were burned. It contains an unknown quantity of incinerator residue. Burning operations ceased in the 1960s because of citizen complaints of odor and smoke. The burn pits were reportedly cleaned out and removed. Subsurface soil samples were collected from the site by the U.S.G.S. in August 1982 and May of 1983. Limited investigations have been completed. Surface soil, subsurface soil, and groundwater samples have been taken. Detections above SCOs of pesticides, metals, VOCs, SVOCs, and PAHs were encountered. Additionally, fill piles containing what is assumed to be lime cleanout waste and pesticides were sampled. Contaminants include: Chloropicrin and corrosive waste. VOCs and metals were detected in groundwater, including Tetrachloroethene contaminants of concern for the site are 1,1-dichloroethene, 1,1-dichloroethane, 1,1,2 trichloroethene, benzene and toluene. Soil investigations revealed elevated metals and VOCs above SCOs including iron, copper, chromium, benzene, petroleum hydrocarbons, and 1-1-1 TCA. Soil samples also had detections of PCBs and PAHs.  Fill piles identified on-site included high detections of chloropicrin, which is a VOC/pesticide that does not have a corresponding SCO. Measured pH in the fill piles was 12.5 in some areas.      Potential exposures will need to be re-evaluated.

narrative: This nine acre site is located immediately south of Buffalo Avenue between 55th and 56th Streets. The Robert Moses Parkway is located to the south between the site and the Niagara River. The site contains facilities for the treatment of residuals from the Niagara Falls Wastewater Treatment Plant, which is located immediately east of the site. This site is a former wetland area that was filled to reclaim land to facilitate construction for the city and chemical plants. (Filling activities have extended the shoreline of the Niagara River up to 1000 feet south relative to its original location). The shoreline extension is attributed to three different filling operations: 1) disposal of refuse, incinerator residue and non-combustibles by the City of Niagara Falls from the 1930s to the 1950s; 2) disposal of dredged material from the construction of the Niagara River Ice Canal by the New York Power Authority (NYPA); and 3) disposal of rock from the Niagara Power Project conduit excavations by NYPA from 1958 to 1963.   The Contaminants of Concern include incinerator ash, lead waste, and organic chemical contamination from the neighboring S-Area landfill owned by Occidental. Numerous investigations were completed at this site between 1982 and 1996. Studies indicate that site soils and groundwater are contaminated with both organic and inorganic compounds, including chlorinated benzene compounds (S-Area VOCs), numerous PAHs and pesticides, and heavy metals. Soil cleanup guidance and groundwater standards were exceeded for numerous contaminants. It has been determined, however, that these contaminants are not present in consequential amounts or are being addressed by measures already in place and that the site does not present a significant threat to the environment.    S-Area VOCs in groundwater were found to be present exclusively in the southern half of the site. This contaminated overburden groundwater is being captured by the S-Area overburden drain collection system installed by Occidental as part of the S-Area remediation program (see Site No. 932019A). Remaining contamination in the soil is being managed under a Site Management Plan.

narrative: The Stauffer Chemical, Whittaker Subdivision Site is located the Town of Lewiston, New York. The site is approximately 1.92 miles northeast of the intersection of Upper Mountain Road and Military Road on the north side of Upper Mountain Road.  The site is also adjacent to the Tuscarora Indian Reservation to the East.This site is referred to as Love Canal North because the trench itself dates back to William T. Love and his excavations in the early 1890s. His efforts to build a power canal resulted in to large excavations, one on the upper Niagara River, which became the infamous Love Canal and 102nd street Sites, and the other at this location. The canal was never joined in the middle.The excavation was approximately 100 feet wide, 2,000 feet long, and 10 feet deep, and trended north-south from the edge of the Niagara Escarpment (which trends east-west in this area) to Upper Mountain Road. It began in the area where Upper Mountain Road currently exists and extended three blocks (1800 feet) north past Escarpment Drive to the edge of the Niagara escarpment. From 1930 to 1952, an estimated 50,000 to 75,000 cubic yards of asbestos, concrete cell parts, reactor linings, scrap sulfur, graphite, scrap metal, slag, phosphates, fluoride containing flux, silicon, zirconium and titanium oxides, flux containing fluorides, cinders, and phenols, reportedly were disposed of in the canal. The canal was covered and residential homes were built on top of the canal.These wastes were largely generated by Niagara Smelting, a subsidiary of Stauffer Chemical Company. There are resident reports that Union Carbide allegedly disposed of material in the canal. Local residents reported seeing Union Carbide trucks dumping brown sludge into the canal, and one resident reported that wastes splattered from a Union Carbide truck and damaged the paint on his car. The canal is visible in aerial photographs dated 1951. Waste disposal was reportedly discontinued in 1952, and the canal was then filled with cinders and slag, as well as white and yellow material (USEPA, 1979). One to 2 feet of fill possibly cover the canal, and many driveways and street beds allegedly are underlain by slag (E&EE, 1989).U.S.E.P.A. directed an investigation of the site in May and June of 1979.  A Phase I Investigation was completed in 1989.  Limited data is available on groundwater quality.  The direction of groundwater flow is uncertain but presumed to be north towards the escarpment.  Sulfate, chloride, nitrates, cyanide, fluoride and phenol were found in groundwater in the old canal areas. A Preliminary Site Assessment (PSA) was also completed in December 1992. With the exception of a sample collected at 1169 Upper Mountain Road, authorities concluded that the results did not meet the definition of hazardous waste. The Upper Mountain Road sample contained PCBs at a concentration of 26 ppm and mercury at a concentration of 132 ppm. Generally, groundwater standards have been exceeded for trichloroethylene, antimony, chromium and lead.  Surface water standards were exceeded for phenol, 4-methyl- phenol, zinc, cyanide, arsenic, lead and mercury.  Based upon the results of the PSA investigation, the original site boundaries were modified to include only 1169 Upper Mountain Rd. The site was delisted from the Registry in 1995.The presence of brown-stained sediment in on-site drainage ditches,and similar material in basement sumps overlying the canal,suggests leachate is being generated and migrating from the canal.Analysis of the basement sumps indicated the presence of PCBs, butat levels below what is considered hazardousAlthough at the time of the investigation at least ten homes in this residential development were built on top of the former canal area, authorities assumed at least one foot of clean fill covers the wastes. The residents were supposedly advised on how to minimize their exposure to subsurface contaminants.Residents at this site use municipal water. The Tuscarora Indian Reservation residents, however, largely rely on private wells and springs as their sole source of drinking water. There is no groundwater data for this site or from wells on the reservation to evaluate the potential significance of this route of exposure.

narrative: The Airco Speer Carbon-Graphite site is located at Packard Road and 47th Street in the City of Niagara Falls, Niagara County on three parcels of property totaling 62 acres.The site consists of a former electrode-manufacturing plant, including a 29-acre disposal area near the center of the property where placement of industrial fill likely occurred. The principal product manufactured at the site was graphite electrodes that were used in electric arc furnaces to manufacture steel and chemicals. Electrodes were manufactured at the site since 1930, when the Speer Carbon Company and Exelon Company each acquired an equal interest in the site from the International Graphite and Electrode Company.  The Speer Carbon Company obtained full ownership of the site in 1932.  The Speer Carbon Company was purchased by the Airco Carbon Company in 1961, and became a division of Airco in 1962, which was later purchased by other conglomerates.Most of the buildings associated with the former manufacturing plant have been demolished. The vast majority of the site is covered with pavement or remains of building foundations. Niagara Metals currently occupies the site.Approximately 20 acres of the site is underlain by a landfill that was used in the past to dispose of manufacturing wastes generated on-site. The fill consists of carbonaceous furnace insulation, asbestos materials, spent refractories and non-repairable equipment. After landfilling, in 1954, various manufacturing operations were built. An on-site electric network of transformers and capacitors was also erected to manage the distribution of electricity to the electrical furnaces.The main contaminants of concern are PCBs and PAHs. Certain testing revealed low levels of twelve volatile organics, 22 semi-volatiles, and 16 pesticides. Subsurface soil samples revealed Aroclor 1248 at a concentration of 59 milligram per kilogram (mg/kg).  Acetone was detected in 6 of the subsurface samples at concentrations ranging from 0.023 mg/kg to 0.13 mg/kg. The sump liquid samples were collected from the interior sumps located on-site.  One sump sample was found to have lead concentrations of 18,900 microgram per liter (g/l).  The source of the lead was not determined.Goundwater samples were not collected at the site. The data gathered during the PSA investigation in 1993 did not establish a significant threat to the environment.

Cayuga Island is in the Niagara River at the outlet of Cayuga Creek in the city of Niagara Falls. The site itself is approximately 5-acres and located in the Niagara River in the southeastern portion of the city of Niagara Falls. The site originally consisted of two areas, the western tip of the island and portions of the southern shoreline, however, after initial investigations only the western tip was identified as the site. The site is bounded by the Niagara River to the north, south, and west; with the remaining portion of the island to the east. The site is located approximately 0.65-miles west of the intersection of West Rivershore Drive and South 86th Street.The site is relatively flat and approximately 6 to 8-feet above the level of the Niagara River. There are several residential dwellings with grass covered lawns and residential hardscape features with West Rivershore Drive splitting the tip of the island from east to west.Prior to 1930, the western end of Cayuga Island was extended west by approximately 250-yards into the Niagara River by the placement of fill and industrial materials. From 1958 to 1962, the western end was then widened by the placement of fill and industrial material reportedly sourced from Carborundum, Union Carbide, Hooker Chemical Corporation, Olin, and Pittsburgh Metallurgical.There is brown silty topsoil overlying fill material comprised of varying materials, including brick, ash, cinders, glass, concrete, and slag.Preliminary site assessments were done in 1992 and 1993. Subsurface soil samples collected from portions of the southern shoreline showed slightly elevated levels of polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs) and metals. Subsurface soil samples collected from the western portion of Cayuga Island showed elevated levels of PAHs, pesticides, polychlorinated biphenyls (PCBs), and metals at a few isolated locations. Sampling also showed elevated levels of PCBs, mercury, and lead. In 1993, the New York Department of Health (NYSDOH) collected surface and subsurface soil samples that confirmed the presence of elevated levels of pesticides and mercury in surface and subsurface soil. Nonetheless, the site was delisted from the Registry of Inactive Hazardous Waste Sites in 1995.Soil is contaminated with mercury, lead, BHCs and other organic chemicals.  Most of the  contamination is in subsurface soil.  The residents whose yards have subsurface soil contamination have been advised not to disturb the contaminated soil by digging or excavating.  However, in a few instances, contaminants were found in surface soil and garden soil at concentrations which might pose a concern if the residents were repeatedly exposed to them.  In these instances, the residents were advised on how they might minimize their exposures to surface or garden soils.Additional monitoring would be needed to confirm the extent and rate of contaminant migration; therefore, the potential for contaminant migration is indeterminable.Additional information about this site is forthcoming.

narrative: Niagara Recycling (Sanitary Landfills) is located at the Allied Niagara Falls Facility on 56th St. in Niagara Falls, NY.  It is located in an industrialized area with Packard Road to the North, Niagara Falls Blvd, to the south, Rail lines to the west and the NYS 190 expressway to the east.Site Features:The main site features consists of numerous active and closed landfills containing both hazardous, non-hazardous and municipal wastes within the boundaries of the adjacent sites.Historical Uses:The 10 acre landfill is the oldest of the Sanitary Landfills (I&II) at the site and received municipal and industrial waste from 1972 until 1984.  These units were closed and capped in 1987.  The landfills were constructed as a series of distinct cells with no recompacted clay liner and no leachate collection system.  A leachate collection system and perimeter channel was later constructed by Niagara Recycling to stop leachate breakouts on the south slope of the landfill.  Monitoring of the leachate quality from the site is required under a discharge permit issued by the City of Niagara Falls.  New landfill cells are constructed as necessary by Part 360 standards.  A number of site perimeter monitoring wells are monitored on a long-term basis under the RCRA Site Monitoring & Assessment Program.Contaminants of Concern (Including Materials Disposed)Contaminant Name/TypeCHLORINATED HYDROCARBONSSite Environmental AssessmentNature and Extent of Contamination:Based on investigations conducted as part of the RCRA Corrective action process and Routine monitoring, the Primary contaminants are VOCs and Metals contained in the landfill leachate.Soil: The facilities are closed sanitary landfills which have been capped in accordance with NYSDEC approved plans.  IC are in place to prevent public access and exposure.Groundwater: The subject facilities have a monitoring and maintenance plan to address groundwater  and leachate monitoring.  Landfill leachate is routinely removed and treated.Soil Vapor & Indoor Air:  There are no structures or receptors since the facility is a closed and capped landfill surrounded by an active solid waste disposal facility.The site will continue to be monitored and maintained as part of the post-closure permit.It is recommended that continued monitoring for chlorinated hydrocarbons in the groundwater take place.  A permit has been issued by the City of Niagara Falls for the discharge of sanitary leachate to the city sewer.  Monitoring of leachate quality occurs regularly as part of this permit.Site Health AssessmentThis site is within the 385 acre CECOS facility which is fenced and has 24-hour security to prevent trespassing.  Ground and surface water, sewer discharge and air emissions are being monitored in and around the site in compliance with permit regulations.  The area is served by public water so exposures to contaminated groundwater are not expected.  Surface water eventually empties into the Niagara River, via the arterial waterways flowing through and around the site.  All discharges to the sewage system are treated on-site at the wastewater treatment plant prior to discharge into the City of Niagara Falls sanitary sewer.  The closure and capping eliminated any potential exposure pathways, however, contaminated groundwater merits continued monitoring.

Prestolite Co. acquired the facility in the 1960s and retooled operations for the manufacturing of hard rubber battery cases, filling of batteries with sulfuric acid, and battery charging. narrative: Occidental Chemical Corporation's (OCC) Buffalo Avenue Plant, located at 4700 Buffalo Avenue, was a major manufacturing facility in central Niagara Falls. The Niagara Scenic Parkway (formerly Robert Moses Parkway) and the upper Niagara River are adjacent to the facility on the south. Vacant land, the New York Power Authority conduits, and other chemical manufacturing facilities are to the west. A distributor of industrial gases and a waste-to-energy facility are north of the site. TheS-Area EPA Superfund site (#932019A), N-Area, and V-Area, residential and light commercial areas, and the Niagara Falls Drinking Water Treatment Plant are east of the site. A populated residential neighborhood is adjacent to the east (56th 63rd streets, as well as Stephenson to Devlin)Chemicals have been manufactured at the site since the very early 1900s. Hooker Electrochemical Company, Oldbury Electrochemical Company, and Niagara Alkali Company operated on various parcels of the current plant site until Hooker Chemical acquired the companies. The companies produced chlorine, caustic, and hydrochloric acid. The mercury cell method was used to separate sodium and chlorine in brine, which was obtained from salt mines in central and western New York. A wide range of chlorinated organic chemicals and compounds were also manufactured beginning in the 1920s, with production of these compounds peaking from the 1940s to the 1970s.Hooker was acquired by Occidental Petroleum Corporation in 1968.It eventually became the Occidental Chemical Corporation Main Plant. Occidental manufactured over 250 different chemical products, including halogenated benzenes, toluenes, phenols, and aliphatics. Over the years, the plant site grew from the original seven acres in 1911 to approximately 130 acres, with hundreds of buildings. Occidental currently owns the facility. In August 2021 Occidental announced an end to chemical production at the facility. The facility is in the process of decommissioning all process equipment and razing buildings.Chemical raw materials, products and wastes have been buried or spilled at numerous locations on the plant site.Bedrock groundwater flow under natural conditions is northwest toward the adjacent lower Niagara River. However, manmade influences have resulted in a complex and changed flow pattern that has altered groundwater direction. Those influences include the New York Power Authority conduits west of the site, the large Falls Street Tunnel (an historic sewer tunnel carved into the upper bedrock approximately 1,800 feet north of the facility, and which intersects the conduits), and remedial groundwater extraction points. After addressing these shifts, groundwater flow in bedrock is now toward extraction wells located along the north and west boundary of the facility. Overburden groundwater flow is primarily toward groundwater collection systems (re-purposed sewers and drain-tile systems) located along the northern and southern boundaries of the facility.The aforementioned manmade Falls Street Tunnel draws portions of the upper Lockport bedrock groundwater flow from seven hazardous waste sites, including this site.Soil and groundwater contamination at the facility is widespread. The site requires engineering controls to contain contamination. The facility is divided into designated areas (based on historical manufacturing) and, aside from the river-adjacent S-Area, the most significant sources of contaminants are located in the C-Area, D-Area, F-Area, M-Area, N-Area, U-Area, T-Area and the Mercury Cell Area. The hazardous waste is present in the soil and groundwater as aqueous (dissolved) phase contaminant plumes and as non-aqueous phase liquids (NAPL).Groundwater contamination remains extensive at the site. In terms of groundwater contamination, Aqueous phase contamination (APL) has been observed in both overburden and bedrock groundwater. Containment is required to prevent off-site migration of the aqueous-phase plume in the overburden. The extent of the aqueous-phase bedrock plume is considerably greater. Contamination in the upper 125 feet of bedrock extends from the facility to the former Falls Street Tunnel, and to the New York Power Authority (NYPA) conduit drains which are cut deep into the bedrock near the western boundary of the property. The extent of the overburden and bedrock NAPL plumes are largely confined to the site, particularly with the use of hydraulic pumps or wells.A network of groundwater and monitoring wells and collection stations are installed throughout and around the site.There are categories of chemicals mainly found in the soil, including: NAPL, dioxins, elemental phosphorus, and mercury. NAPL has been detected beneath the B, C, D, F, N and U-Areas of the plant. Areas of NAPL contamination are removed when found and when feasible or are otherwise contained. Specifically, contaminants of Concern (Including Materials Disposed) include:There are at least 41 inorganic elements and organic compounds contaminating the site, as well as elements such as phosphorus, arsenic, mercury, and lead. The organic compounds can be grouped into classes as follows: toluene and chlorotoluenes; benzene and chlorobenzenes; chloroethenes; chlorobenzotrifluorides; chlorinated cyclic organic compounds; chlorinated pesticides (including Mirex and Lindane); chlorinated and non-chlorinated organic acids; and 2,4,5-trichlorophenol. Dioxin, as a by-product of manufacturing 2,4,5-trichlorophenol, is also present on site.Dioxin is present above 10 ppb beneath portions of the D, M and X-Areas of the plant and at 1-10 ppb beneath portions of the E, F and U-Areas. Areas of dioxin contamination were capped in 1992.In August 2021 Occidental announced an end to chemical production at the facility. The facility is in the process of decommissioning all process equipment and razing buildings.In 1989, EPA and DEC issued a report prioritizing 33 site clusters in order of theirpotential for polluting the Niagara River. The 33 site clusters were divided into three categories.This site was designated as a Category I priority site with estimates of greater than 50 lb/day loads of pollution to the Niagara River.Sites from Category I and II collectively represented 99.9% of the total estimated loadings of 694 lbs (315 kg)/day. Reports from 2023 indicate that chemical waste continues to migrate into the Niagara River from a sewer at the site.

narrative: The Occidental/Hooker Chemical S-Area site is an 8-acre industrial landfill owned by the Occidental Chemical Corporation (OCC). It is located at the southeast corner of OCC's Buffalo Avenue chemical plant in Niagara Falls, New York, along the Niagara River. Until it was moved one parcel over in 1997, the citys drinking water treatment plant was next to this site. The site is located in an industrialized area of Niagara Falls. There is also a large residential community within 1/4 mile of the site.The landfill lies atop approximately 30 feet of soil, clay, till, and manmade fill on an area reclaimed from the Niagara River. Beneath these materials is fractured bedrock.OCC admitted to disposing of at least 63,000 tons of chemical wastes into the landfill from 1947 to 1961, including organic phosphates, acid chlorides, phenol tars, thionyl chloride, chloridic, trichlorophenol, benzoyl chloride, liquid disulfides and chlorotoluene-based disulfides, metal chlorides, thiodan, chlorobenzenes, and miscellaneous chlorinated hydrocarbons. These estimates are based on incomplete records. These wastes were both liquid and solid. Most wastes were disposed of in drums, but some liquids (DNAPL) were placed directly in trenches from tanker trucks. Two lagoons for nonhazardous waste from plant operations were located on top of the landfill and were operated under New York State permits until 1989, when OCC discontinued operating these lagoons.	Priority pollutants include:      trans-1,2,-Dichloroethylene      Chloroform      Trichloroethylene      Benzene      Toluene      Chlorobenzene      Phenol      Dichlorobenzenes      Hexachloroethane      Hexachlorobutadiene      Hexachlorocyclopentadiene      Hexachlorobenzene      Carbon tetrachloride      Trichlorophenols      Mirex      1,1,2,2-Tetrachloroethylene      Nonpriority pollutants include:      Trichlorobenzenes      Tetrachlorobenzenes      Monochlorotoluenes      Dichlorotoluenes      Octachlorocyclopentene      Pentachlorobenzene      During an inspection of the citys drinking water structures in 1968, chemicals were found in the bedrock water intake structures. In 1978, further sampling of the structures and bedrock water intake tunnel revealed extensive chemical contamination in the tunnel and the forebay. Drinking water contained tetrachlorobenzene (TCB). After congressional hearings and a lengthy sampling plan, the contamination was traced to this site. Chemicals migrated into the Niagara River, and surrounding soils and groundwater. Subsequent investigation at the site found that the property underneath the drinking water plant was contaminated by the migration of S-Area contamination.      In 1989, EPA and DEC issued a report prioritizing 33 site clusters in order of theirpotential for polluting the Niagara River. The 33 site clusters were divided into three categories. This site was designated as a Category II priority site with estimates of between 1 to 50 lb/day loads to the Niagara River.      Sites from Category I and II collectively represented 99.9% of the total estimated loadings of 694 lbs (315 kg)/day.      Remediation actions included: a 7-acre cap with a perimeter drain collection system, groundwater APL purge wells, NAPL extraction wells, a treatment facility, and more.The City of Niagara Falls Drinking Water Treatment Plant (DWTP) was moved further east to another neighboring property (end of 1997), 29 years after S-Area contamination was first discovered in the intakes. The former drinking water plant area is referred to as the V-Area.      There are ongoing investigation, operation, monitoring, and maintenance activities at the Site.      The S-Area Landfill is historically significant because the phrase "non-aqueous-phase-liquid" (NAPL) was allegedly first used here.

narrative: The Chemours Plant (former DuPont Plant Site) is an approximately 52.0-acre site located in an industrial area on Buffalo Avenue in the City of Niagara Falls, Niagara County. It is bordered by Buffalo Avenue to the north and the Robert Moses Parkway, which is adjacent to the Niagara River, to the south. The "a-f" designations refer to sub-areas, historical Operable Units (OUs), or remedial segments. The site has a long history of major industrial operations and chemical production. The site was built on fill underlain by old river-bottom sediments of silt and clay overlying Lockport Dolomite. The depth to bedrock is approximately 10 ft.Gill Creek divides the site into approximately equal sections to the east and west of the stream channel. Over half of the site is built on filled land. There are also residential areas north of Buffalo Avenue.The Chemours Plant was in operation from 1896, when the Niagara Electro Chemical Company began the manufacture of metallic sodium. E.I. du Pont de Nemours and Company acquired the plant in 1930 from R&H Chemical Company and manufactured products of both organic and inorganic chemical composition until 2016, when DuPont ceased operations in Niagara Falls.In 1982, investigations confirmed the presence of chlorinated organics in the groundwater. The prime contaminant of concern is trichloroethylene. Others include 1,1,2,2-tetrachloroethane, trichloroethylene, 1,2,4,-trichlorobenzene, benzene, chloroform, trans-1, 2-dichloroethylene, methylene chloride, trichloroethene (tce), tetrachloroethylene, toluene, vinyl chloride, metal cyanide sludges, hexachloroethane, trichlorofluoromethane, and BHC. Studies also verified contamination on the plant site and deep in the bedrock. Off-site migration of contaminated groundwater has occurred. Moreover, Gill Creek, which bisects the site and empties into the adjacent Niagara River, was heavily contaminated. It was partially remediated in 1982. The remaining creek remediation was completed in 1992 under a Consent Order.The manmade Falls Street Tunnel draws portions of the upper Lockport bedrock groundwater flow from seven hazardous waste sites, including this site.DuPont initiated a remedial plan to control the migration of contaminants from the plant site that involved the collection of groundwater from the overburden and shallow bedrock zones and treatment of collected water. The plan also uses the Olin Production Well, that is now operated by DuPont, to collect groundwater from the deep bedrock zones.Long term operations, management, and monitoring activities are in place to collect, treat and monitor groundwater remedial systems from the overburden and bedrock zones including the Gill Creek remediation. In summary, between 1992 and the present, multiple improvements have been made to the collection system including: treatment system upgrades, adding pumping wells, and installing blast fractured bedrock trenches with pumping wells.The plant site was determined to be a major source for contaminant migration.

narrative: The Hooker-102nd Street Landfill site is a 22-acre site located on the Niagara River at 102nd Street, at the eastern edge of the City of Niagara Falls, Niagara County. It is bounded by Buffalo Avenue to the north, the Belden Site (a.k.a. Niagara River Site# 932055) to the east, the Niagara River (and Cayuga Island, a residential community) to the south and Griffon Park (another waste site) to the west. Homes are across the street and nearby to the east. Occidental Chemical Corporation, formerly Hooker Chemical and Plastics Corporation, owns 15.6 acres. Olin Chemical Corporation owns the remaining 6.5 acres.Hooker/Occidental and Olin estimate that from 1943 until 1970 they dumped approximately 100,000 tons of hazardous waste at the 102nd Street dumpsite, most of which wasat surface, meaning not buried. Those wastes included: 1,2,4,5-tetrachlorobenzene, BHC Cake (includes Lindane), chlorobenzenes, Phosphorus, mercury brine, Hexachlorocyclohexane (all isomers, including 300 tons of hexachlorocyclohexane process cake, including lindane), benzene, Mercury, Mirex, 1,4-dichlorobenzene, 1,2,4-trichlorobenzene, organic compounds (SVOCs) such as phenol and polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs), polychlorinated biphenyls (PCBs) and dioxins. The highest concentration of dioxin ever found to date in New York State was identified there. A highly contaminated city storm sewer that originated at Love Canal ran through the middle of the site and emptied into the Niagara River delta.In 1989, EPA and DEC issued a report prioritizing 33 site clusters in order of theirpotential for polluting the Niagara River. The 33 site clusters were divided into three categories. This site was designated as a Category II priority site with estimates of between 1 to 50 lb/day loads to the Niagara River.Sites from Category I and II collectively represented 99.9% of the total estimated loadings of 694 lbs (315 kg)/day. Reports from 2023 indicate that chemical waste continues to migrate into the Niagara River from the site.The site was listed on the National Priorities List (NPL) by the EPA in 1983. Remedial construction was completed in 1999. Groundwater monitoring wells are present around the perimeter. Leachate recovery and pump chambers are located along the Niagara River. Collected leachate is automatically pumped north to the Love Canal site for treatment. Non-aqueous phase leachate (NAPL) recovery wells dot the central portion of the site. The site includes a sub-surface perimeter slurry wall and a synthetic landfill cap (1997), which is now 29 years old.The site was delisted from the NPL by the EPA in August 2004. Operation and site management is ongoing. EPA took the site off the National Priorities List in August 2004.

The Belden site is a residential property located at 2006 Wildwood Parkway on the boundary of the City of Niagara Falls and Town of Wheatfield, New York. The site is located in a residential neighborhood on the Niagara River. This site was used by the Goodyear Company for the deposition of fill, rubble, and thiazole polymer blends in unknown quantities.      Leachate has been noted leaving this site in surface water, but thechemical composition is unknown.      Soil samples at the site were analyzed for volatile organic compounds (VOCs), semi-volatile organic compounds, metals, and pesticides. Metals, VOCs and BNAs were detected in soil samples collected at the site; however, the only compound detected above residential use soil cleanup objectives was mercury. Mercury was detected in one soil sample at 7.39 parts per million (ppm), above the residential use soil cleanup objective of 0.81 ppm.      A USEPA investigation concluded that there was no imminent or substantial risk to public health.  However, this investigation did not cover the southwestern section of the site where contamination is suspected. There are no barriers or signs restricting access to this poorly covered, overgrown site. Duck hunters have been observed on-site behind a duck blind.  Leachate has been noted, thus creating the possibility for human exposure.      Preliminary data indicate some potential for contaminant migration, butanalyses of ground-water samples indicate low concentrations of contaminants.Additional analyses would be needed to define the extent of ground-water contaminationand the potential for offsite migration. The potential for contaminantmigration is indeterminable.   Further sampling is needed so that potential human exposures to site-related contaminants can be assessed.

The 4.2 -acre Town-owned site is listed as an inactive hazardous waste site (No. E932135) and was found to contain contamination from volatile organic compounds (VOCs), semi-volatile organic compounds (SVOCs) and Polychlorinated Biphenyls (PCBs) in soils that were above established standards. Landfilling of the property in the late 1970s and early 1980s raised the elevation of the site up to10.5 feet in some places. The fill material consists of industrial wastes such as ash, cinders, firebrick, coal, foundry sand and slag. In addition, unknown slag-like material and an oily sheen on the groundwater surface and within the fill have been found, but not identified through laboratory analysis. It is also reported that the southern portion of the property was filled in with grinding wheel sand, extending the land approximately 100 feet to the south.      The landfill is located within the Town of Wheatfield, Niagara County on land that was reclaimed from the Niagara River channel in the area of the Niagara River north bank and Williams Road extension.  The site was operated from 1965 through 1972.  During this time period the landfill received solid waste primarily from Carborundum's Wheatfield and Buffalo Ave.  plants and Bell Aerospace Textron, of Niagara Falls.  The site also received approximately 25 loads of ash from the City of Niagara Falls incinerator. Other fill material disposed of on site consisted of broken abrasive wheels, fines, adhesives, fly ash, and miscellaneous debris and rubbish.  Organic chemicals are still present. Initial investigations were inconclusive; clean up is needed. Potential impacts on the Niagara River need to be further evaluated.

This site is also known as 2040 River Road and the Lynch Park site. It is located in the town of Wheatfield, proximate to the Niagara Falls boundary. It was also adjacent to the 200-unit Lynch Trailer Park and several residences.The land the site is located on was reclaimed from the NiagaraRiver channel. narrative: Niagara Falls Air Reserve Station is of the worst polluted military sites in the nation with PFAS. Per- and polyfluoroalkyl chemicals are present in groundwater at the station in levels up to 300,000 times greater than drinking water standards set by the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency. The pollution came from foam, called aqueous film-forming foam, or AFFF, that firefighters used mostly in training activities at the station from the 1960s through late 1990s. PFAS chemicals have since made their way into Cayuga Creek, according to studies by Buffalo Niagara Waterkeeper and the state Department of Environmental Conservation. Cayuga Creek runs through the property and is a tributary of the Niagara River and Lake Ontario, a major drinking water source for tens of thousands of people in the United States and Canada. Clean up has not yet commenced.      Building 850 on the Station property is a large maintenance hangar for the aircraft under the 914th Air Force Reserve Airlift Wing. The hangars fire suppression system went off unexpectedly on August 21, 2010, releasing approximately 48,000 gallons of fire suppression foam (FFF foam). Most of the foam was contained in the hangar; however, some leaked outside into a neighboring tributary that runs into Cayuga Creek. The spill incident report requested no further action. NYSDEC concurred and the case was closed September 21, 2010. Knowledge of PFAS chemicals subsequently changed. The EPA issued health advisories for PFAS categories (PFOA, PFOS) beginning in January 2009.

The 64th Street North Site is located in an urban area to the north of Pine Ave. at the northeast intersection of Factory Outlet Blvd and ------Drive in Niagara Falls, Niagara County.Approximately 60 percent of this land is covered by pavement or commercial buildings.Since the late 1930s, the area now known as the 64th Street site has been used intermittently for the disposal of municipal, commercial, construction/demolition, and alleged industrial and hazardous wastes. This disposal has taken place within drainage swales crossing the site and within surrounding wetland areas.Between the late 1930s and the 1950s, the 64th Street-North Site has been used for the disposal of municipal waste from the City of Niagara Falls and construction and demolition waste, and possibly incineration waste, from a nearby Department of Defense (DoD) housing facility. Citizens noted dumping by a local waste hauler as well. International Paper and Goodyear Tire and Rubber Company wastes were disposed of on the Johnson-owned portion the 64th Street-North Site. Waste disposal occurred from 1955 to the early 1970s.Testing confirmed hazardous waste and lead contamination exceedances; but further testing did not replicate those results, so no further action was taken.The Basic Carbon site, besides being a possible Hazardous waste site itself, was also part of the 64th Street-North site.In the late 1950s through the early 1960s, the I-190 was constructed and now bisects the 64th Street North site.

The Harper Substation is located on Royal Avenue in the City of Niagara Falls, New York. It is a 25-acre rectangular parcel that is surrounded by industrial facilities to the north, east and south. Homes are 300 feet away. The twin buried conduits of the New York Power Authority Power Project lie to the west and the Citys Falls Street Tunnel, a large combined sewer, lies to the north. Both systems influence groundwater flow on the siteThe substation was originally constructed in the early 1920s by the Niagara Falls Power Corporation (a predecessor to Niagara Mohawk, and National Grid Company).  Two former Buildings (Echota and Terminal Buildings) were demolished between in 2000.      PCB-containing oil was historically used at the substation.A preliminary investigation in 1999 revealed contaminated soil and subsurface structures. Remedial activities were undertaken. Groundwater beneath the site is contaminated with chlorinated ethenes and dichlorobenzenes from a source upgradient of the site. In addition, LNAPL containing PCBs, VOCs and SVOCs was detected in one upper bedrock monitoring well.The site no longer contains significant amounts of contamination.

narrative: Sabre Park (EPA ID: NYD030222103) is located at 1705 Third Avenue (also known as 1705 Factory Outlet Boulevard / Fashion Outlet Boulevard / Third Avenue Extension / Connection Boulevard), Niagara Falls, NY 14304. The site encompasses a 34-acre former mobile home community that was owned by Union Carbide from 1949 to 1969, then became a mobile home community in 1972 with approximately 250+ housing units. In September 1978, Amherst Paving - under contract to Hooker Chemical - inadvertently deposited contaminated fill from Hookers property at Sabre Park during site expansion work. The fill contained chlorinated solvents, mercury, and heating oil. EPA sampling in 1986 and 1988 found elevated mercury concentrations. NYSDEC listed the site as an Inactive Hazardous Waste Disposal Site in 1989. EPA subsequently excavated approximately 1,200 cubic yards of mercury-contaminated fill classified as hazardous waste (D009-mercury). NYSDEC delisted the site in 1995. The property later became part of the Fashion Outlets of Niagara Falls expansion (FONF Expansion BCP). NYSDEC BCP documents reference contamination in the Sabre Park parcel from perched water mixing with slag and fill material, with elevated metal concentrations and pH anomalies in groundwater. The sites administrative history is complex due to multiple name changes and overlapping remediation programs.
